Meeting header
Date: 2025-07-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Sentinel CTO), Aisha Rahman (ML Eng), Tom Wu (Infra)
Recording id: ff-20250703-sentinel-0091

Auto-generated summary:
- Goal: scope a 4-week POC to validate latency and cost for Sentinel's real-time enrichment pipeline using Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoints + SDK integration.
- Success criteria discussed: 95th perc latency < 250ms for 2k concurrency baseline, prediction cost reduction >= 30% vs current infra, structural JSON outputs for downstream rule engine.
- Next steps: benchmark plan, SDK examples, infra deep-dive, draft POC SOW and pricing.

Topics: workload sizing, benchmarks, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, SDK integration, tool/function calling patterns, structured output (JSON schema), timelines and SLOs, security & data residency notes.

Partial action items (auto): Jordan to send benchmark spreadsheet link; Priya to provide SDK snippets and function-calling demo; customer to provide traffic sample.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): "Hey everyone, great to meet you. Quick roll call?"
[00:05] Carlos (Sentinel): "Carlos here, Aisha and Tom on too. Thanks for setting this up."
[00:10] Priya (Redwood-SE): "Hi all, Priya from Redwood, I'll lead the technical scope. We'll focus today on the POC shape: what you want to measure, what data you can share, and integrations — SDKs vs direct OpenAI-compatible calls."
[00:30] Carlos: "High level — we run a real-time enrichment service for alerts. At peak we see about 800 rps across the inference tier, but what matters is burst concurrency; typical sustained 300 rps. Latency at the moment spikes to 600-800ms which is painful for our downstream rules. We'll want 95th perc under 250ms ideally."
[00:50] Aisha: "Our models are a mix: a short-context 1k token classifier for entity normalization and a medium-context 2k token template generator. We also do tool-calling: we hit internal APIs for enrichment, and we'd like the model to return structured JSON that maps to our rule engine fields."
[01:10] Tom: "On infra — we run in GCP, private VPC, with strict egress rules. Any POC needs to respect our VPC peering and KMS keys. Also SOC2 and audit logs are needed for our procurement."
[01:30] Jordan: "All good. For a POC we'd propose two tracks: 1) integration/latency validation using Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoints (simple to integrate), and 2) an SDK path where you use our SDK for function-calling and structured output orchestration. We can run a side-by-side benchmark against your current stack."
[01:50] Priya: "Quick note: by OpenAI-compatible we mean REST shapes and params that mirror OpenAI so your devs can switch endpoints with minimal changes. We also support an SDK with helpers for function-calling and schema enforcement — it will emit structured JSON and validate the output where possible."
[02:10] Carlos: "Sounds promising. For success criteria — beyond latency — we need accuracy retention. If we quantize or use cheaper variants, any output regression must be < 2% on our metric. Also cost per inference target: 30% reduction is the business goal."
[02:30] Priya: "We can run model variants: full fp16, 8-bit quantized, and a mid tier. Our benchmark harness will compute latency distributions and run your eval prompts to check delta in F1/accuracy. We'll include automatic rollback recommendations."
[02:50] Tom: "Network topology: will we route through a public endpoint or can Redwood accept connections over a VPC peer? Egress is blocked by default. We need to know firewall rules and IPs or set up private connectivity."
[03:10] Jordan: "We offer Private deployment and dedicated capacity. For a quick POC we usually start with hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoints over TLS; if you need private peering we can shift to a private plan — that adds a bit of lead time. We'll capture the options in the SOW."
[03:30] Aisha: "About SDK: do you have language support? We use Python and Go; we also have a Node microservice for ingestion."
[03:40] Priya: "Yes — Python, Go, Node SDKs. The SDK includes a convenience function for tool/function calling so you can register an internal enrichment API and Redwood will call it as a tool with typed inputs. We have sample code that shows function signature definition and returning structured JSON."
[04:00] Carlos: "Any gotchas with streaming? We want streaming for the template generator to display partial outputs in UI."
[04:10] Priya: "Streaming is supported on both endpoints and SDK. Streaming semantics mirror standard chunked responses — but note that for function-calling we buffer until tools complete unless you opt into intermediate events. Also prefix caching and KV cache are available for repeated contexts to reduce cost; sometimes the transcript says K-V cash which is wrong in the export, ha."
[04:40] Jordan: "For the benchmark plan, we'll need: 1) a one-week sample of production traffic (anonymized) — token counts, prompt shapes, avg seq lengths, concurrency patterns, 2) a list of evaluation prompts for accuracy checks, and 3) SLO targets (latency, cost, correctness)."
[05:00] Carlos: "We can export a CSV. We'll need to scrub PII — Aisha will handle. Timeline-wise we aim to start the POC by July 14 and run 3-4 weeks."
[05:15] Priya: "Ideal. We'll scope two phases: baseline (week 1) to reproduce current metrics on our hosted endpoints; tuning & quantization (week 2) to assess cost/quality tradeoffs; integration & automation (weeks 3-4) for SDK-driven tool-calling and structured output validation. If private peering required, that extends lead time by ~2 weeks for network setup."
[05:40] Tom: "Procurement will ask about compliance — any PCI/PHI concerns? We don't handle PHI but there are regulatory logs. Do you provide audit logs and KMS integration?"
[05:55] Jordan: "Yes. We support KMS/HSM for key management, detailed audit logging, SAML/SSO, RBAC. We'll share SOC2 and our security handbook. For the POC we can limit log retention and sign an NDA if needed."
[06:10] Aisha: "For structured JSON, can the SDK assert a schema? We need a fixed schema to feed our rule engine: fields like entity, confidence, timestamp, enrichment_source."
[06:25] Priya: "The SDK can take a JSON schema and we run an output parser that tries to enforce the schema. We also return a \"parse_confidence\" metric so you can detect off-schema responses and trigger fallbacks. We'll include examples where the model returns a nested structure mapping to your rules."
[06:45] Carlos: "Tool calling: we want the model to call our enrichment API when needed, otherwise return cached values. Do you support asynchronous tool calls?"
[06:55] Priya: "We support synchronous tool calls in the request flow, and also an async pattern where the model outputs a tool invocation record that your service picks up and processes; we have examples for both. For async we recommend idempotency tokens and a small queue for eventual consistency."
[07:15] Jordan: "Benchmarks we'll run: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens, and downstream throughput with our batching config. We'll also run evals for your accuracy metrics across model variants."
[07:35] Aisha: "One more constraint — our rule engine expects exact field names. If the model slightly renames fields, it's a pain. Can Redwood enforce canonical keys?"
[07:45] Priya: "Yes — the SDK includes a schema wrapper that can map synonyms to canonical keys and will fail the call if required fields missing. We can also run a post-processor to normalize results."
[08:05] Carlos: "How invasive is SDK adoption? Our ingestion code is in Node and we have a microservice that calls inference. Ideally we just swap endpoints and tweak some param names."
[08:15] Priya: "If you use OpenAI-compatible REST calls, it's minimal: change endpoint and set an API key. The SDK provides helpers but is optional. For function-calling the SDK reduces engineering work by handling registration and validation automatically."
[08:30] Jordan: "I'll note three POC configurations for the SOW: Hosted OpenAI-compatible quick path; Hosted + SDK for function-calling and schema enforcement; Dedicated/private deployment if peering or compliance required. Pricing will differ — quick path lowest friction, dedicated has committed cost."
[08:50] Tom: "Any example numbers for cost savings? Even rough ballpark will help with procurement."
[08:58] Jordan: "We typically see 20-50% cost reductions depending on batching and quantization. For your workload with many short requests, batching helps less but KV/prefix caching and shorter token sequences can drive ~30% by using smarter routes and smaller variants."
[09:20] Aisha: "On the benchmark harness — will you run it in our VPC or remotely?"
[09:28] Priya: "We can run both: run synthetic load from Redwood to your endpoint to measure end-to-end latency; or run a local agent in your VPC that hits a Redwood sandbox if you prefer private connectivity. For initial work we usually do hosted measurements to get quick signals."
[09:45] Carlos: "We heard about function calling security concerns — can you restrict which tools are callable?"
[09:52] Priya: "Yes. The function registry is explicit; you only register approved functions and you can scope them by role. Calls include signed ids and we log full request/response for audit. We'll share a sample registry definition."
[10:05] Jordan: "Let's talk timeline — you said start July 14. We'll need the traffic CSV and eval prompts one week before so we can prep harness. So target to have inputs by July 7; Redwood deliveries: benchmark plan by July 6, SDK snippets by July 8, SOW draft by July 9."
[10:25] Carlos: "That's doable. Procurement might push back on network peering; if they do we'll stick to hosted testing first."
[10:35] Aisha: "Question: when you run quantized variants, how do you ensure deterministic outputs for our evals?"
[10:42] Priya: "Quantization can add nondeterminism; for evals we fix random seeds where supported and run multiple seeds to compute variance. We'll report statistical significance and recommend variants that meet your regression thresholds."
[11:00] Tom: "Can you also provide traceroutes or region info? We need to know which GCP regions you'll target to keep latency low."
[11:07] Jordan: "We'll aim for us-west1 / europe-west1 depending on your region. For private deployments we can place dedicated capacity within your VPC region. We'll include region mapping in the benchmark plan."
[11:25] Carlos: "Any blockers on our side? We'll need procurement and security to sign the POC SOW and accept the risk assessment."
[11:32] Jordan: "We'll provide SOC2 and a tailored data handling appendix. For the POC we can sign a limited SOW and NDAs. I'll loop in legal if needed."
[11:45] Priya: "Technical recap: we need traffic sample CSV, eval prompts, desired schema for structured output, and network constraints. We'll provide SDK examples for Python/Go/Node, a benchmark harness, and a model variant matrix with expected CPU/GPU types."
[12:05] Carlos: "Ok let's finalize next steps. Carlos will own providing data, Jordan will send benchmark plan and SOW draft, Priya will send SDK samples and function-calling demo video link."
[12:20] Jordan: "I'll email the benchmark spreadsheet and a short deck with POC options. Also linking the security pack: (link) — we'll add SSO/KMS docs. Priya will attach SDK repo link in follow-up."
[12:35] Aisha: "Small ask — include a minimal end-to-end demo that shows function-calling to our enrichment API and returning the structured JSON so our PMs can see it."
[12:45] Priya: "Yes, we'll include a recorded demo and a minimal Node example that you can run locally."
[12:55] Jordan: "Great — thanks everyone. We'll send notes and next steps. Any last questions?"
[12:59] Carlos: "No, thanks. Looking forward to the benchmark."
[13:02] Jordan: "Thanks, bye."
